claims.claim: Reviewers mention a steep learning curve and find certain mechanics or paths forward confusing for new players.

citations.review_text: There is a fairly steep learning curve, unless you've played other resource-gathering/ base building games.  That being said, I'm kind of a moron, but I still figured things out, and ended up really enjoying the game.. (or at least, I kept coming back, day after day).  Overall, alot of fun.

7 Days to Die has got me HOOKED! I've played lots of Survival and Zombie games, but this one has so much going for it: Great design, graphics, characters, sense of tension, danger, and accomplishment, intense fighting, great building and crafting options, tons of varied strategy, exploration, and the gift of retaining all your spoils and regaining health after being killed! Sometimes the path forward or details like Repair are confusing, but experimenting or searching works it all out. Bravo, developers. A game to love by people who love gaming!

claims.claim: Reviewers state that the game is too expensive at its current price point and suggest waiting for a discount.

citations.review_text: good but expensive i would wait for a discount

At 45 bucks.... nah. I wanted to play with my friend but i got this game when it was dirt cheap. No clue why it's so expensive now. Mostly for the mods I saw on Youtube. The general game is like a 15 dollar quality.

How am I supposed to get my friends to buy this game when it's a janky zombie game thats years old priced at 45$ and looks like hotdog water. This is not worth 45$. Lower the game back down to like 10 - 15$ where it should be and people will come back. I used to be a big fan of this game and its development but it's like the pot of greed spawned in the Fun Pimpz office and robbed them of all logic. Weird game designs, story telling so bad the fans have to come up with ideas, mods that outclass the game designers by people who dont even get paid... Everywhere you turn there is something apparent. Lazy and greedy devs doing near the bare minimum just to keep people buying instead of actually listening to fans. I hope something changes

claims.claim: Reviewers describe experiencing severe technical performance issues including frame rate drops that strain hardware and crashes.

citations.review_text:
7 frames to kill my gpu and 7 days to build a maxed out underground base just for it to be destroyed like a sand castle.

Note: did anyone else get that notification that said "I'm leaving you and taking the kids i hate you i hate you i hate you"? Funniest thing I've ever seen 😂😂😂😂

The Good:

What can I say about 7 Days to Die.  The game itself is quite good and offers plenty in the way to keep you busy and entertained, providing you like zombie shooters.  Almost everything in the game can be destroyed for resources, to build your base and level up your character, the map from what I have seen of the game is quite large, and there are different biomes to explore, the traders in the game offer missions and rewards for completing those said missions, some of which can be quite fun, the graphics aren't going to win any awards, but you have to take into consideration, the amount of CPU and GPU processing power it takes to run the voxel based engine 7 Days to Die is built on.  The music score can be atmospheric when it decides to play, and the controls and combat system are what you would expect from a game like this.

The Bad

Out of all the games I own, over 300 at this point on various platforms and have ever played, I have never come across a game as badly optimised as this one.  In my first three hours of play, the game crashed over 60 times.  I have spent more time going online and researching different graphic settings, how best to optimise the graphics to keep crashes limited, I have a modern powerhouse of a PC and the game struggled in places.  I finally had to write a value to the registry for the TDR and set it to 10, which did work and stopped the crashes, but oh no, it wasn't over, the game decided it wouldn't connect to Epic online services, and wouldn't even let me play offline, I had to completely remove the game from my system and the registry, everywhere I found it on the computer.  I reinstalled, and it decided to work.  Great finally I am going to get to play the dam thing, then it decided it didn't like my save game file, and just like that 23 hours of game play lost.  So I cannot recommend this game, it is the buggiest mess I have ever owned, and the devs should be throughly ashamed of themselves for ever releasing it li…

claims.claim: Reviewers note that character progression and crafting are tied to finding or buying random books and recipes through RNG.

citations.review_text: This game has what is possibly one of the worst gameplay loops to ever exist. The progression system being tied to random ass books that you have to buy/find through RNG completely ruins a potentially amazing game.

followed this since 2015 
you butchered it
everything has turned into grind and no reward 
there's no actual point for scavenging just random paper and cloth fragments till you get bored tf out 
went to the hospital looking for an antibiotic and found like 2 bandages with 50 zombies, struggled for 3 hours to realize its just easier to slime my own character 
the buildings have improved since then its a bit scarier than before since zombies stay asleep unless they are triggered from close but still if you know that your reward is gonna be needed like 100 times, would you really  spend one hour clearing a big area just for a small advancement ?
When you don't have enough content it only damages your base users to milk everything out of them to keep them in the game back then i gave it a good 2 week playthrough, now it got as soon as i started to see the changes 
no end game no sense in doing random boring quests. Doing "clear area, dig ground and search, search area" doesn't really ring "interesting" to me 
not gonna mention how you stopped your modders from fixing what you broke 

probably no one said it to you guys but yes you lost to DayZ time to wrap it up

cohorts.summary: Longtime survivors note clunky controls, shifting progression systems, and optimization issues alongside complaints about the price.

claims.claim: Reviewers state that the current price tag of $45 is too high for a game that has been in development for many years.

citations.review_text: I have almost 1700 hours in this game and been playing it off and on for +-10 years. I love it and will always be my go to. TFP thank you for brining us a game worth while. That being said, development has been extremely slow over the years and at the current price tag of $45 I cannot justify telling others to purchase. $45 is a rip off. Wait for a sale if you want it that badly.

Good game but im not going to recommend based on the insane price tag.  This game is 13-14 YEARS old.  It has been plagued by performance issues for multiplayer even up till the present date. I have some 600 hours on this game. It is fun, especially so with friends, but $45? Nope.  Go buy Ark survival evolved on sale for dirt cheap, or valheim, or the amazing Palworld (massive updates). There are way better survival games at bargain prices.  Seriously, who came up with this price tag?  

Instead  of pumping out crappy DLCs, how about optimizing the game for multiplayer and adding QOL features that the modding community has carried on their backs all these years? How about lowering the price a little for a game that is 13 years old and has been held up by early supporters?

Really fun game. As you can tell, I've got lots of hours. I like the customization of the game as well. My only issue is after over a decade in Alpha, they're now working on it, which is great news, but slow going with any updates and trying to charge $45 for a game that's not changed much since the last Alpha. Some of the changes don't make any sense either like the random storms. It offers no benefit and I just have sit inside a building while watching YouTube on my phone until it passes. I had to turn it off. Thankfully I can. Just saying, the game is worth around $20 to $25 for sure, but at $45, they are really reaching there.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the combat, movement, and general controls as feeling clunky and awkward.

citations.review_text: Ridiculously fun. Tons and tons of stuff to do. Aesthetically pretty nice looking and unique too. Combat and movement and sort of everything feels clunky and awkward but strangely satisfying at the same time, in just the right sort of balance that makes it endearing but occasionally frustrating. I think that the lighting isn't the best though. It looks kind of washed out, and even with the darkness turned down quite a bit it's still easy to see in the middle of the night, or in a dark building with the lights completely out. I get that we don't want like, Skyrim ENB where you can't see anything, but I want that experience of walking around a building in the dark and feeling really kind of helpless. The horror aspect of it all could be brought up a good bit, I guess.

1498 hours in, and I can confidently say 7 Days to Die is one of the most addictive survival games I’ve ever played.

What keeps me coming back is the perfect mix of base building, looting, crafting, and that constant tension of the blood moon hordes. Few games capture that feeling of “just one more day” like this one does. Whether you’re reinforcing your base at the last second or scavenging a POI that goes sideways fast, it never really gets old.

The full release feels like the most complete version of the game so far. The visuals are cleaner, progression is more structured, and there’s a lot more polish compared to earlier builds. It still has its quirks here and there, but honestly, that’s part of the charm at this point.

It’s also one of the best co-op survival experiences out there. Playing with friends turns every horde night into chaos in the best way possible.

If you enjoy survival games with depth, creativity, and a bit of jank that somehow makes it better, this is absolutely worth your time.

1498 hours later… and I’m still not done.

claims.claim: Reviewers state that character progression and skill advancement depend heavily on finding books and magazines through random looting.

citations.review_text:
RECOMMENDED BUT NOT AT THIS PRICE

I've been playing since the alpha days, which means I've experienced nearly the entire lifespan of the game. It's easily one of my favorite survival-crafting games, and there's a lot here to enjoy. However, it's hard to ignore some of the long-standing issues that have persisted for years.

My biggest frustration is the direction the developers have taken with certain design choices and their apparent lack of responsiveness to community feedback. There are problems that players have been asking to have addressed since alpha, yet many of them remain unresolved.

The UI is another major weakness. For a game that has been in development for this long, it feels outdated and lacks the level of customization that many players expect from a modern survival game.

Finally, the progression system centered around finding books and magazines feels like a step backward. Having so much of your character's advancement tied to random loot drops can make progression feel more dependent on luck than on actual gameplay and effort.

782 hours played.

I've been with this game since its early Early Access days, and that's exactly why this review hurts to write.

The biggest problem is that the game has gradually abandoned what made it unique in the first place.

The new skill progression system based on finding and reading books makes absolutely no sense. Instead of learning through experience, practice, or survival, your character becomes stronger because they happened to find the correct piece of literature. It feels artificial, gamey, and completely disconnected from the world.

At the same time, traders have become the center of the entire gameplay loop. Sure, giving them quests sounds useful on paper, but now you're constantly running errands just to unlock progression. Survival, resource management, inventory decisions, and the feeling of struggling through a hostile post-apocalyptic wasteland have all been pushed into the background.

What used to be a survival sandbox now feels like a chain of mandatory tasks.

One of the things I loved most about the older versions was the freedom. You could go almost anywhere from the beginning. Some areas were more dangerous, some required better equipment or preparation, but the world was open to you. The game trusted you to make your own decisions.

Now entire portions of content are locked behind masks, reputation requirements, unlock chains, and quest progression. Instead of exploring because you're curious, you're exploring because the game has finally granted you permission.

The result is a much more restrictive and arcade-like experience.

Every update seems to add another layer of artificial progression while removing the sense of freedom, danger, and discovery that originally made the game special.

Maybe new players won't notice the difference. But after 782 hours, having watched the game evolve from its earliest versions, I can honestly say that I find it less engaging, less immersive, and significantly less enjoyable than it used to be.

…

My general observations are the game has a somewhat steep learning curve that rewards long term commitment; it can be punishing early on but higher player levels are a lot of fun to play. Enjoyable gameplay loop that offers a lot of customization to suite your desired experience. The survival-horror aspect is fairly well done, with a larger emphasis on the survival aspect. World has enough of a backdrop and lore to provide a small narrative foundation, but leaves plenty of room to role play a bit and integrate yourself into the world; and in my opinion this is all best experienced when playing with friends. 

The greatest example of this is how leveling up solo vs in a group plays out... Playing solo, the magazine and book system is entirely convoluted, and general skills are far to broad to level up in an enjoyable fashion. If you level up skills to build vehicles, you forgo skills dedicated to cooking, or tool crafting, etc. You're constantly selling yourself short, by design and not of your own fault. Enemy scaling is tied not only to leveling up, but also by how long you exist in the game world. So you can get to end game difficulty, and will still be missing very important skills which can make it a real struggle. 

The game innately reinforces building an individual class, which makes much more sense when playing with a group. You can delegate which magazines and books go to certain classes amongst your group. You are now able to focus in on specific skills pertinent to your class, while your crew focuses on others, so that overall no one is missing out on other equally important skills. One is the chef, one is the mechanic, one is the engineer, etc. Going about the game as a group just feels like the intended way to play, and would prove to be true because it's much more fun to do so.
